reader: AI reader 3 (targeted check at the stated place, papers read in the app's browser)

results.note: Results › Plasma Methamphetamine and d-Amphetamine Levels › Acute Effects: peak concentrations for both drugs 3–4 h after administration; Results › Cardiovascular Effects › Acute Effects: peak cardiovascular effects within 15 min; Methods › Participants: 13 male volunteers. Nuance: blood was sampled only up to 240 min (Methods › Procedure), so the 3–4 h peak sits at the last two sampling points.

results.corrected_locator: Whole paper (no F statistic or degrees of freedom anywhere; Methods › Data Analysis names the ANOVAs only); Methods › Procedure › Sample sessions (urine screen excluded amphetamines and THC); Discussion, outpatient limitation
results.note: Content correct. There is no 'Statistical analysis' heading (it is 'Data Analysis'), and the urine-screen statement is in Methods › Procedure › Sample sessions, not in the analysis section. The Discussion itself notes that participants may have used drugs outside the laboratory undetected by standard urine toxicology (raised for the residual cardiovascular effects). Results report only p-value thresholds.

results.corrected_locator: Methods › Design (outpatient); Methods › Procedure › Sample sessions (urine screen excluding amphetamines and THC); Discussion, outpatient limitation; Results › Cardiovascular Effects › Residual Effects (next-day heart rate); Figure 1, upper right panel
results.note: No 'Participants and urine screens' section exists; the Participants paragraph has no urine-screen text. Text parts confirmed: 10-session outpatient study; screen excluded amphetamines (and THC); authors note possible undetected use outside the laboratory; next-day heart rate 86.1 ± 1.9 after 12 mg methamphetamine and 90.5 ± 3.4 after 50 mg d-amphetamine (placebo 76.8); the Acute Effects text prints no heart-rate values. The by-eye acute peaks (about 80 and about 86) were not re-read: Figure 1 is an image and this round does not use screenshots of figures.

Pharmacologic actions of methamphetamine, 2nd paragraph: raises extracellular dopamine, serotonin and norepinephrine by promoting release from nerve endings; the author writes that how release occurs is not completely understood but appears to involve redistribution from vesicles via VMAT2 to the cytoplasm and reverse transport through the plasma membrane transporter. The Figure 2 legend gives the same mechanism for dopamine only (via the dopamine transporter), hedged as 'likely'.

Table 3 (values in parentheses are age-corrected): caudate 7.0 ± 1.2 vs 8.7 ± 1.6 and putamen 6.7 ± 0.9 vs 8.3 ± 1.4, both marked significant vs controls; 19.5% and 19.3% lower. The legend applies 0.8% per year (no decline in the first 10 years) and itself notes this rate may be somewhat high. Uncorrected values: caudate 5.8 vs 7.5, putamen 5.5 vs 7.3.

results.corrected_extracted: Striatal binding of (+)[11C]DTBZ, a VMAT2 probe historically used to assess dopamine-terminal integrity, was 28% higher than in 22 controls in 28 users scanned a mean 2.6 days after last use, which the authors read as low stored dopamine rather than more VMAT2; in the 17 who stayed abstinent to a second scan (mean 9.8 days) it did not differ from controls, and it was not decreased at either scan.
results.note: Results › PET Results (first two subsections) and Table 3: full striatum 3.09 vs 2.41 (+28%, p<0.0001); second scan 2.54 in 17 abstainers vs 2.46 in 9 rescanned controls (p=1.0). The anchor overstates in two ways: what rose was binding of a probe the authors treat as sensitive to vesicular dopamine (the Discussion cautions against reading it as a change in VMAT2 protein), and the 10-day normalisation covers only the 17 abstainers; the 7 who relapsed had 17% higher first-scan binding and were not rescanned.

results.corrected_extracted: Utah cohort: HR 2.8 (1.6–4.8) for a Parkinson's disease code on or after the first methamphetamine/amphetamine code, 15 vs 27 events (3 of the 15 on the same date; excluding same-date diagnoses, HR 2.2, 1.2–4.0); see the Parkinson's disease claim in section 9 for the validity concerns.
results.note: Abstract › Results and Results §3.2 give HR 2.8 (1.6–4.8); Table 2 gives 15 vs 27. 'Later' overstates: Results §3.2 says the subsequent outcome deliberately included diagnoses on the same date as the first exposure code, and Table 2 row 3a (event time > 0) leaves 12 vs 27; the sensitivity HR without them is 2.2 (1.2–4.0).

Table 2, Last use and PET columns (month/year): 8/95→12/95 = 4, 7/93→1/97 = 42, 5/93→2/97 = 45, 12/93→4/97 = 40, 3/91→8/96 = 65, 11/96→4/97 = 5 months; mean 201/6 = 33.5 months. The abstract gives an average abstinence of about 3 years (methamphetamine and methcathinone users together); dates are month-level only.

results.corrected_locator: Results › Mapping cortical gray-matter deficits and › Lateralization of cingulate deficits (11.3%, 0.7%, 3.6%); Results › Hippocampal deficits (7.8%); Results › Whole-brain gray- and white-matter measures (white matter, total grey matter); Methods › Participants and Table 1 (22 vs 21)
results.note: All numbers correct: right cingulate 11.3% lower (p<0.05); left 0.7% (p=0.4 in Mapping, p>0.1 in Lateralization); medial frontal 3.6% (trend, p<0.1); hippocampus 7.8% smaller (p<0.01). But the white-matter excess (7.0%, p<0.01) and the null total grey matter (p>0.1) are in the Whole-brain section, not in the two sections named.

Table 1: education 15.2 (SEM 0.50) vs 12.8 (SEM 0.42), p<0.001. Table 2: smokers of more than 5 cigarettes a day 2 of 21 vs 15 of 22 (chi-square significant). Table 3: Beck Depression Inventory 1.25 (SEM 1.25; n=20) vs 9.77 (SEM 1.89; n=22). After converting SEM to SD, d ≈ 1.13 (education) and 1.14 (depression). No analysis adjusts for education, smoking or depression; the hippocampal regressions adjust for age, sex and brain size, and the marijuana sensitivity analysis is the only other check. Methods › Participants calls the education gap slight.

Results §3.2 and Table 2. Control non-smokers > control smokers only in the right orbitofrontal cortex. Control non-smokers > methamphetamine smokers in 10 clusters. Control smokers > methamphetamine smokers in 4 clusters: left superior temporal, right inferior temporal, right supramarginal, left precentral. Of these four, only left precentral has a same-named cluster among the ten. All FWE-corrected for cluster extent, p<0.05. Groups: 18 control non-smokers, 25 control smokers, 39 methamphetamine-dependent smokers (Abstract).

Table 2, Control Nonsmoker > Methamphetamine-Dependent Tobacco Smoker block: exactly these ten clusters (precentral left and right), FWE-corrected for cluster extent; the same list is in the Results §3.2 text (p<0.05 FWE-corrected). Covariates were age, sex and marijuana-use frequency (Methods §2.4).

results.corrected_locator: Discussion, limitations (2nd paragraph); Methods §2.4 (covariates: age, sex, marijuana use); Methods §2.1 (4–7 days abstinent); Methods §2.2 (residential stay with daily urine toxicology)
results.note: Content correct. In the limitations paragraph, results with education in the model supported the main results only at a more liberal p<0.005 uncorrected threshold; the authors argue that education is entangled with methamphetamine use and that mothers' education did not differ. 4–7 days of abstinence is in §2.1, but the urine verification (daily urine toxicology during a residential stay at the UCLA clinical research centre) is in §2.2, not §2.1.

results.corrected_extracted: Days abstinent: mean 6.64 (SD 5.2), printed only in the mood table, where the footnote ties it to the time of the mood assessment; the paper does not state the interval at scanning or describe how abstinence was established or verified.
results.note: Table 3 (Beck Depression Inventory block), footnote b: depression scores correlated with days of abstinence at the time of assessment. Nowhere does the paper say the MRI was done at that interval, so 'at scanning' goes beyond the text. Methods › Participants and › MRI scans mention no urine testing or other verification (selection criteria are referred to London et al. 2004).

Table 1 (peak VAS ratings, 50 mg vs placebo): jittery 24.82 vs 7.36, sweating 25.09 vs 2.09, heart beating faster 43.18 vs 11.27, nose burning 28.00 vs 2.60, each marked significant vs placebo (P<0.05). Values are peak ratings; 11 participants in a 2-week inpatient study (Methods › Participants).

Results › Cardiovascular Effects › Acute Effects: relative to placebo and the 12-mg doses, both 50-mg doses increased heart rate, systolic and diastolic pressure (p<0.01 for all comparisons); methamphetamine raised heart rate more than d-amphetamine (p<0.05). Table 2: summed 'Stimulated' VAS (max 700) 111 (SEM 49) placebo vs 320 (SEM 47) 50 mg methamphetamine, also above 50 mg d-amphetamine (226). N = 13 men (Methods › Participants).

results.corrected_extracted: Dose effects on the repeated time-course measures are tested with denominator degrees of freedom of 330 (plasma), 240 (cardiovascular) and 180 (visual-analogue ratings), whereas 11 participants give 30 for a dose effect, the value the paper itself uses for the once-per-session drug-effect questionnaire items; so the printed p-values for the time-course measures overstate precision. The differences in Table 1 are large enough that the direction of these effects is not in doubt.
results.note: Results › Plasma Methamphetamine Levels F(3, 330); › Cardiovascular Effects F(3, 240) for heart rate and blood pressure; › Subjective Effects F(3, 180) for the VAS items, but F(3, 30) for the questionnaire items on desire to take the drug again and willingness to pay. The anchor implies the paper never uses the correct 30. Table 1 prints F-values for planned comparisons without df. Eleven participants (Methods › Participants).

results.corrected_extracted: No F statistics or degrees of freedom are printed (only p-value thresholds), and the one results table (Table 2) lists only subjective-effect items with significant effects; Figure 3 shows selected ratings.
results.note: Whole Results text has no F or df. The paper has two tables, and Table 1 is the study design, so 'the tables' overstates: only Table 2 reports effects, introduced in Results › Subjective Effects › Acute Effects as the additional statistically significant VAS and DEQ effects; every row in it carries at least one significance mark.

results.corrected_extracted: The abstract says depressive and psychotic symptoms resolve within 1 week. The Results do not support this for depression (scores fell over 2 weeks and stayed above controls through week 3) and only partly for the self-reported psychotic-symptom subscales (falling in week 1 and reaching control levels by the end of week 2). Analyses use 25–32 of the 56 participants, and the numbers assessed at weeks 3–5 are not given. Participants were admitted for neuroimaging studies lasting 2 or 5 weeks, so data after week 2 come only from the 5-week studies (study card: design, attrition, key finding 6 note).
results.corrected_locator: Abstract › Findings and Conclusions vs Results › Depressive symptoms and › Psychiatric symptoms; Table 2 title and Figure 1, 2 and 4 legends (n = 32, 28, 26, 25); Results › Demographics, last sentence; Methods › In-patient milieu
results.note: Depression: BDI fell substantially over the first 2 weeks, stayed above controls during the first 3 weeks (P<0.05) and approached them only at the end of week 4 (P=0.07). BSI subscales fell during week 1 and reached control levels by the end of week 2, yet the same paragraph says users scored higher than controls at most time points. The rest is correct. Demographics says n<56 for each analysis, legends give one n per measure with no per-week counts, and the 2- or 5-week neuroimaging stays are in Methods › In-patient milieu. Table 1 is demographics only.

Table 2 (n = 32; mixed-effects time effect over days 1–14): 33 rows (3 vital signs + 30 symptom items). Significant at P<0.05 with no correction: red/itching eyes, no motivation, increased appetite, sleep difficulties, tired or low energy, the item on people watching or talking about the participant, the item on often thinking about taking methamphetamine, and reduced sexual pleasure (8). Craving P=0.79, depressed P=0.26; loss of interest was borderline at P=0.06.

results.corrected_extracted: All participants reported use within the 7 days before admission and had to be active users with a methamphetamine-positive urine screen at entry; they were non-treatment-seeking, paid volunteers with other current Axis I disorders excluded, which the card judges biases toward fast resolution.
results.corrected_locator: Methods › Participants; Methods › Methamphetamine Withdrawal Questionnaire (MAQW) (7-day statement); Discussion › Limitations of current study
results.note: The 7-day use is reported as a characteristic of all participants (in the MAQW subsection, with discrepant self-report and urine cases excluded from analysis), not stated as an inclusion criterion; the stated entry requirement in Methods › Participants is active use with a positive urine screen. Non-treatment-seeking, compensated, other current Axis I diagnoses excluded: confirmed. The Limitations themselves say findings may not generalise to treatment seekers, whose withdrawal may be more severe or longer.

Results › Psychiatric symptoms and Figure 4 legend: BSI scores, n = 25 users vs 85 controls; panel B psychoticism and panel G paranoia (the legend says 'Paranoia subscale'), effect of duration of abstinence P = 0.003 each, with scores falling over the first week. The distress-vs-diagnosis point is the card's own note; the paper presents the BSI as self-report psychopathology indices.

Abstract; Table 1a (4,935 exposed, 24,675 matched controls); Table 2 (PD 15 vs 27; PD/PT 30 vs 49); Results §3.2 (HR 2.8, 1.6–4.8; PD/PT HR 3.1). Nuance: the PD/PT interval is printed as 1.9–4.9 in the Abstract but 2.1–4.5 in Results §3.2; the anchor gives no interval for 3.1.

results.corrected_extracted: Absolute risk of a Parkinson's code: 0.30% of the exposed cohort vs 0.11% of controls over a mean follow-up of 6.8 years (controls 7.1), about 2 extra cases per 1,000.
results.note: Editors' calculation checked against Table 1a and Table 2: 15/4,935 = 0.304%, 27/24,675 = 0.109%, difference 1.95 per 1,000. Table 1a gives mean follow-up 6.8 years (SD 4.3) for the exposed cohort but 7.1 (SD 4.3) for controls, so 6.8 years does not apply to both groups.

Results §3.1, last paragraph and Table 2 (4 vs 22 PD/PT events; footnote b: only one exposed cocaine case had code 332.0); Table 1a (1,867 vs 9,335 controls); Results §3.2 says no increased risk, with outcomes extremely limited and estimates imprecise. The hazard ratio is printed only in Figure 2 (an image of a table-style forest plot, viewed this round): cocaine vs controls HR 0.9, P=0.85, 95% CI 0.3–2.4. The 'location to be confirmed' caveat can be dropped and Figure 2 added to the locator.

Table 1a, last two rows: age at index PD/PT diagnosis median 49 (25–69) vs 44 (20–68); years to diagnosis mean 2.0 (SD 1.8) vs 2.9 (SD 3.5). Results §3.1, last paragraph: based on a limited subset of medication data, 3 exposed users and 5 matched controls with incident PD/PT had a carbidopa–levodopa pharmacy order (controls had 49 PD/PT cases, Table 2).

Methods §2.2.2: 16,931 with a METH/AMPH code and no HIV indication; 11,985 with other illicit drug or alcohol codes and 11 with prior PD/PT removed, leaving 4,935. Methods §2.2.3: 7,952 cocaine-coded without HIV; 6,084 with other drug or alcohol codes and 1 with prior PD/PT removed, leaving 1,867. The percentages (70.8% and 76.5%) are editors' calculations; the paper prints counts only.

Results §3.2, 2nd text paragraph (after Figure 1): METH/AMPH vs cocaine HR 3.9 (1.4–10.8), P=0.01, also in Figure 2 (image, viewed). The tobacco-adjusted result is printed as HRtobacco=1.9 with an interval reading 0.9.4.0, P=0.01, data not shown. An interval spanning 1 alongside P=0.01 is itself inconsistent, which supports reading the numbers as garbled.

results.corrected_extracted: Up to 25% of people first diagnosed with drug-induced psychosis develop a primary psychotic disorder after some years, with even higher figures for methamphetamine-induced psychosis; a 2008 review found 18 papers on the characteristics or outcomes of substance-induced psychosis, 7 of them on stimulants, and only one of those 7 had a 1-year follow-up.
results.note: Risk factors and acute vs. chronic psychosis, 5th paragraph (ref 100 for the 25%, ref 67, a Thai first-hospitalisation cohort, for methamphetamine; ref 101 = Mathias, Lubman and Hides 2008). The anchor's '1 of 18' is wrong: the sentence says 7 of the 18 papers were on stimulants, but only one had a 1-year follow-up, which most naturally means one of the 7. It also drops the 'after some years' qualifier.

results.corrected_extracted: Second-hand: Japanese researchers, as the review reports, have argued that amphetamine psychosis can last up to several years, and describe spontaneous relapses after remission; stressful situations seem to trigger these in susceptible individuals.
results.note: Prevalence and clinical presentation, 4th paragraph (refs 64–66 for duration; refs 67–70, including a Thai cohort, for the stress trigger and vulnerability factors). The review presents duration as what Japanese researchers have argued, not as clinical series, and hedges the stress trigger (it seems, in susceptible individuals). The same paragraph says acute amphetamine psychosis usually recovers faster than schizophrenia and is hard to distinguish from a primary psychosis triggered by amphetamine.

§3.5 and Table 2: methamphetamine use disorder, cross-sectional, unadjusted OR 3.46 [2.04, 5.89], 2 studies, Q 0.00, I² 0% (fixed-effect, per the table footnote); one adjusted estimate, OR 2.80 [1.40, 5.90], from Lin et al. 1996 (ref 11), a study of male–male twin pairs who served in the US military. §3.6: no eligible longitudinal studies. Drug class: Table 1 lists Lin 1996 under methamphetamine use disorders as a lifetime DSM-III use disorder without naming the drug class, so this still needs checking in Lin 1996. The Abstract gives this single-study 2.80 as the use-disorder finding.

results.corrected_locator: §2.1 Protocol (update of ref 1, McKetin et al. 2019, EClinicalMedicine; PROSPERO CRD42017081893); §2.2 Eligibility criteria (criterion added beyond the protocol)
results.note: Content correct. The Abstract does not say the review is an update. §2.1 Protocol does (and the end of the Introduction), and §2.3 says the May 2017 search was updated in July 2021. §2.2 says that, in addition to the protocol's criteria, only studies comparing levels of methamphetamine exposure were kept, giving the exclusion of comparisons with other drug use as an example.

Table 2, cause-specific rows, Suicide: 6 studies, 40,085 people; CMR 0.20 per 100 PY (0.07, 0.55), I² 98.2%; SMR 12.20 (4.89–30.47), I² 97.7%. The same figures are in Abstract › Findings and Results › Standardised mortality ratios.

Table 1 (thousands): MUD without injection 549 (417–682) 2015, 397 (299–496) 2016, 815 (598–1033) 2019; MUD 741 (2015), 672 (2016), 1091 (2019). Arithmetic: 815/397 = +105%, 815/549 = +48%; 1091/741 = +47%, 1091/672 = +62%. Abstract › Results and Results › Trends in Methamphetamine Use give 105% (from 397 000) and 62% (from 672 000) under a 2015-to-2019 framing, i.e. from the 2016 values. The headline 43% for any use is also from 2016 (1.4 million = 1381).

Table 1 (without opioids: 3220 in 2015, 3956, 4915, 5934, 7051 in 2019; P for trend <.001) and Results › Trends in Psychostimulant-Involved Overdose Deaths (increased 119%, from 3220 to 7051). Deaths are among decedents aged 18–64, ICD-10 T43.6 (Methods › Data Sources).

Both figures are in Discussion › Limitations, the fourth limitation: approximately 85% to 90% of such death certificates mentioned methamphetamine (ref 46); some certificates did not report the specific drugs involved (e.g. 6% in 2019), so mortality may be underestimated. The Methods part of the locator is loose: death data are described under Methods › Data Sources (T43.6, 'largely methamphetamine'), not Measures, and give neither figure.

results.corrected_extracted: Cause-of-death ascertainment was often unclear, and polydrug use could not be examined. Older cohorts (before about 2001) probably involved less methamphetamine relative to amphetamine, including the crystalline form, than recent ones, which the authors could not examine directly. The headline ratio appears as 6.83, 6.3, 6.2 and 6.08 in different places. Of the 23 pooled cohorts, the text accounts for 21 (8 with the authors' own ratios, 13 imputed).
results.note: Discussion › Limitations: unclear cause-of-death ascertainment; patterns of polydrug use and comorbidity could not be examined. On drug type, the paper is relative and hedged: older cohorts may have differed, with likely much more methamphetamine than amphetamine (including crystalline) in recent cohorts, listed as variability they could not examine. 'Amphetamine rather than crystalline methamphetamine' overstates this. Ratio values: 6.83 in Abstract, Table 2 and Results › SMRs; 6.3-fold in the 1st Discussion paragraph (which also says 25 eligible cohorts); about 6.2-fold in the Discussion's opioid comparison; 6.08 (4.41–8.37; n=23) in Results › Sensitivity analyses. 8 author-reported + 13 imputed = 21 in Results › SMRs and Methods › Calculation.

Table 2, cause-specific rows (CMR per 100 PY): drug poisoning 0.14 (0.06, 0.34; 5; I² 95.5%), accidental injury 0.20 (0.08, 0.47; 7; 98.4%), suicide 0.20 (0.07, 0.55; 6; 98.2%), cardiovascular 0.13 (0.06, 0.29; 4; 94.2%), homicide 0.03 (0.02, 0.06; 4; 45.2%). Reporting nuance: Abstract › Findings prints the cardiovascular interval as 0.06–0.55, against 0.06–0.29 in Table 2.

Table 2, GBD region rows: SMR East Asia 4.48 (2.53–7.93) to Australasia 10.52 (9.30–11.89); others 5.09–7.81, with Southeast Asia 7.30 (0.82–65.30) and Central Europe from one study. Results › SMRs: SMRs did not differ significantly by GBD region (and meta-regression found no region effect, Results › Factors associated). Results › Sensitivity analyses: without the single HIV-positive cohort, SMR 6.47 (4.96–8.43) and CMR 1.09 (0.97–1.22).

results.corrected_extracted: Searches covered 2008 to February 2018, with 1980–2007 studies taken from the authors' earlier review; imputed ratios are standardized against general-population rates matched for age, sex, location and calendar years only, with no adjustment for other differences between the cohorts and the general population.
results.corrected_locator: Methods › Search strategy and study screening; Methods › Calculation of crude mortality rates, standardised mortality ratios and risk ratios
results.note: Search: 1 January 2008 to 22 February 2018 in Medline, Embase and PsycINFO; studies published 1980–2007 came from the team's previous review. The 13 imputed SMRs divide the cohort CMR by the GBD 2017 rate for the respective age, sex, location and years, so 'age and sex only' is wrong. The 8 author-reported SMRs used the original authors' methods. No adjustment for other differences is described.

results.corrected_extracted: Prespecified complete-case analysis (participants providing all four evaluation-window samples): stage 1, 15 of 52 (28.8%) vs 9 of 177 (5.1%); stage 2, 13 of 80 (16.2%) vs 1 of 75 (1.3%); overall effect 18.7 percentage points (95% CI 11.6 to 25.8). The denominators mean that only 47.7% of the stage 1 active group and 60.2% of the stage 1 placebo group provided all four samples (editors' calculation: 52 of 109 and 177 of 294), so missing samples were more common on active treatment in stage 1; in the main analysis two or more missing samples, or dropout, counted as non-response.
results.note: Results › Primary Outcome, paragraph after Table 2 and Figure 2: all numbers exact. Stage denominators 109/294 and 114/111 are from Table 2. Methods › Outcomes: participants with two or more missing urine results, or who discontinued, were recorded as non-responders. A single missing sample therefore did not by itself mean non-response (3 of the remaining 3 negative could still count), so 'missing samples, counted as non-response' was too broad. Stage 2 complete cases: 80/114 (70%) vs 75/111 (68%).

ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03078075, read via the registry API (current version). Study Record Dates: first submitted 2017-03-02, first posted 2017-03-13; actual start 2017-05-05, so registered before enrolment. Primary Outcome Measures: two stage-specific outcomes (responders at week 6 for stage 1 and week 12 for stage 2, defined as at least 3 of 4 negative urines; the stage 2 description repeats 'end of stage 1 (weeks 5-6)', an apparent copy error). The article (Results › Primary Outcome; Table 2 footnote) defines the primary outcome as the weighted average with weights 0.43 and 0.57, citing the statistical analysis plan included with the protocol. The plan's date and the registry's version history were not checked.

Methods › Participants: methamphetamine use on at least 18 of the 30 days before consent; opioid-free at randomization; excluded if in concurrent treatment for a substance use disorder. Further requirements: DSM-5 moderate or severe methamphetamine-type stimulant use disorder, and two or more methamphetamine-positive urines at least 2 days apart within 10 days before randomization. Table 1: 26.7 ± 4.1 days of use in the 30 days before consent; most frequent route smoking 293 of 403 (72.7%); 33.5% reported any intravenous use.

Abstract › Results and Results › Participation and Retention: 60 MSM randomized, 30 per arm (20 of 30 and 22 of 30 at baseline, 28 [93%] completers per arm); 56 (93%) completed the trial and final visit; 673 of 780 weekly urine samples (86%) collected (84.9% vs 87.7%, P = .30). Methamphetamine dependence by SCID (DSM-IV-TR) was an eligibility criterion (Methods › Study Participants).

Results › Primary Outcome: Urinalysis Results, 1st paragraph: in the intent-to-treat GEE analysis, the risk of a positive urine decreased faster on mirtazapine, RR 0.57 (0.35–0.93), P = .02, with fitted trends in Figure 2. The 'at 12 weeks' qualifier comes from Methods › Data Analysis: the effect is the divergence of the fitted linear trends at 12 weeks, omitting week 1. Sensitivity analyses gave similar RRs, 0.53–0.62.

Abstract › Results and Results › Primary Outcome, 1st paragraph: final visit 12 of 27 (44%) on mirtazapine vs 17 of 27 (63%) on placebo (baseline 22 of 30 and 20 of 30). The editors' RR recomputes as 12/17 = 0.706, 95% CI 0.42–1.18 (log method).

Results › Secondary Outcomes › Medication Adherence: adherence by medication event monitoring systems (electronic caps) 48.5% (48.3% mirtazapine vs 48.7% placebo; P = .82); self-reported 74.7% (75.9% vs 73.5%; P = .92).

Results › Secondary Outcomes › Safety and Tolerability: no overall difference in adverse-event frequency (P ≥ .99). Reported only in the mirtazapine arm: drowsiness 13 (43% of 30), increased appetite 4 (13%), weight gain 3 (10%; gains of 12.5, 9.5 and 7.9 kg, none discontinued). Two serious adverse events, one per arm, neither judged drug-related.
